Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
649 AM EDT Sat Aug 1 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 218 AM EDT Saturday...

Isolated flash flood threat remains for late Sunday into early 
Monday with slow-moving showers and thunderstorms possible.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 218 AM EDT Saturday...

1. Very Warm Temperatures and Dry Conditions Saturday 

2. Increasing chances for showers and embedded thunderstorms 
Sunday afternoon into Sunday night. Locally heavy rainfall possible. 

3. Daily chances for showers and thunderstorms with temperature 
at or above seasonal normals.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 218 AM EDT Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: No significant weather expected today or tonight. Patchy 
early AM fog may be locally dense in a few of the deeper river 
valleys, but will generally dissipate with PBL mixing between 12-
13Z. A narrow ridge of high pressure will bring mostly sunny and 
very warm conditions to the North Country today. Will see an 
increase in high cloud cover this afternoon associated with an 
upstream upper trough extending from northern Ontario southwestward 
to a closed 500mb low across Iowa. Even with filtered sunshine, 
850mb temperatures of +15C to +16C will support valley highs in the 
mid to upper 80s. Surface winds will become southerly at 5-10 mph 
supported by weak southerly gradient flow. Modest low-level moisture 
advection will generally keep 2-m dewpoints in the mid-60s, 
resulting in humid conditions areawide. 

For tonight...generally quiet and muggy conditions. Inverted sfc 
trough shifts ewd from the Ottawa Valley toward the St. Lawrence 
Valley during the pre-dawn hours on Sunday. This will bring a low 
chance (20-30%) of some rain showers into the St. Lawrence Valley 
before daybreak. Otherwise, looking for overnight lows in the mid-
upper 60s, except locally in the lower 60s east of the Green 
Mountains.

KEY MESSAGE 2: We'll be monitoring the slow-moving upper flow pattern 
Sunday into Monday. Generally looking at a positive tilt mid-level 
trough across sern Ontario, which extends back southwestward to a 
closed low in the Ohio Valley region. Prevailing mid and upper level 
ridge over Eastern New England will result in very slow movement to 
this upstream system, but it appears that forcing will be sufficient 
for isolated to scattered showers by Sunday afternoon, especially 
across nrn NY. Weak mid-level lapse rates support limited 
instability, with narrow CAPE profiles. However, increasing PW 
values, approaching 1.7-1.9" and WBZ heights near 13kft will support 
locally heavy rain with any convective activity that does develop. 

Support for showers and thunderstorms evolves ewd across the 
Champlain Valley and across central/nrn VT during Sunday night into 
Monday. Have indicated high PoPs (80-90%) with widespread showers 
and a few embedded thunderstorms with weak CAPE through the 
overnight hours. Again, thermodynamic conditions don't support a 
severe threat, but locally heavy rainfall is possible. Sfc boundary 
eventually settles south and east of our forecast area late Monday 
afternoon with generally drying conditions from NW-SE. At the 
current time, have indicated 0.5 to 1.0" rainfall with this system 
across most of the North Country, and some amounts locally exceeding 
1.0" in the St. Lawrence Valley. Can't rule out a localized flash 
flood threat, especially given slow movement of inverted trough and 
very high PW values. However, not a strong consensus for heavy rain 
outside the St. Lawrence Valley at the present time, and amounts 
there are currently not expected to be significant enough to produce 
flooding over the prevailing flatter terrain of the St. Lawrence 
Valley. We will continue to monitor, but most sections of the North 
Country will see a period of wetting rainfall late Sunday into 
Sunday night and into the first half of Monday. Drier conditions 
generally return for Tuesday with highs in the low-mid 80s.

KEY MESSAGE 3: A typical late summer pattern looks to set up across the 
region for the second half of the upcoming week. Daily chances for 
showers, with some thunderstorms possible, seem likely as we see 250-
500 J/kg of CAPE each afternoon with weak shear. This should result 
in pulse like showers and thunderstorms that try to develop across 
the higher terrain and lake breezes. There is the potential for a 
round of organized convection towards the end of next week as a cut 
off low over the southeastern US phases with northern stream energy 
and ejects northward quickly ahead of a cold front. However, 
deterministic guidance is all over the place with trying to resolve 
how the southern stream and northern stream energy interact with one 
another. Temperatures each afternoon should easily warm into the 
lower to mid 80s but given persistent cloud cover and shower 
activity, it seems rather unlikely any location will hit 90 degrees 
this week.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z SATURDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/...
Through 12Z Sunday...VFR conditions and light southerly winds
are expected through the forecast period. However, a brief
period of IFR to VLIFR fog will continue to KMPV and KSLK
through 1230Z to 1300Z. Otherwise, high level clouds will stream
overhead and gradually lower to around 8000 ft by 12Z on Sunday.

Outlook...

Sunday: VFR. Chance SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Sunday Night: Mainly VFR, with local IFR possible. Likely SHRA,
Slight chance TSRA.
Monday: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. Likely SHRA, Chance
TSRA.
Monday Night: VFR. Chance SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Tuesday: VFR. Slight chance SHRA.
Tuesday Night: VFR. Slight chance SHRA.
Wednesday: VFR. Chance SHRA.

&&

.BTV WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
VT...None.
NY...None.

&&

$$
